articles.title: Nepal power monopoly yet to commit purchases from 281 projects worth 16,425.77 MW
articles.summary:
As many as 281 hydropower projects with a combined installed capacity of 16,425.77 megawatts await power purchase agreements (PPAs) with the Nepal Electricity Authority, leaving developers who have already invested heavily in surveys and project studies uncertain about their future.

The developers claim to have spent between Rs5 million and Rs6 million per megawatt on survey licences, feasibility studies, environmental assessments and other preparatory works before reaching the PPA stage.

Since hydropower projects typically require at least five years to complete after signing a PPA, industry representatives warn that prolonged delays could create fresh electricity supply challenges in the longer term despite Nepal’s current surplus during the monsoon.

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA)’s data show that among projects which have completed grid connection agreements and are awaiting PPAs are 102 run-of-river schemes with a combined capacity of 2,556.30MW, 31 peaking run-of-river projects totalling 5,276.30MW, and two storage projects capable of generating 1,491MW.

In addition, 122 run-of-the-river projects with a combined capacity of 1,874.88MW, 19 peaking run-of-the-river projects totalling 1,548.29MW, and five storage projects with a combined capacity of 3,679MW have formally applied for PPAs.

Successive governments have delayed signing new agreements since 2022, citing low domestic electricity consumption, inadequate transmission infrastructure and uncertainty over future export markets.

Although projects below 10MW had previously received PPAs almost automatically, even those projects have seen little progress since the last fiscal year.

The delays compounded after last year's budget introduced the ‘take-and-pay’ model for run-of-river projects, replacing earlier arrangements under which the NEA assumed greater purchasing obligations. However, this year's budget has pledged to immediately resume PPAs for projects below 10MW, although implementation has yet to begin.

The issue has resurfaced as one of the most contentious policy debates in Nepal's energy sector.

During Rajendra Lingden's tenure as energy minister, the Cabinet decided in July 2022 to increase the share of run-of-the-river projects in Nepal's overall generation mix from 30–35 percent to 40–45 percent. The NEA board subsequently approved PPAs for up to 1,500MW of run-of-the-river projects based on the order in which grid connection agreements had been completed.

Later, in February 2024, then-energy minister Shakti Bahadur Basnet announced that all run-of-the-river and peaking run-of-the-river projects below 10MW would be eligible for PPAs. Despite those policy decisions, developers say agreements remain stalled.

Because the NEA retains a monopoly over electricity purchases, developers cannot secure financing without its approval.

The authority currently signs PPAs at Rs8.40 per unit during the dry season—from mid-November to mid-May—and Rs4.80 per unit during the wet season.

Developers say the agreements are essential because banks and financial institutions generally refuse to finance hydropower projects unless a long-term buyer is guaranteed.

The NEA, however, says it must evaluate several factors before committing to new PPAs. These include whether the national grid requires additional electricity, whether transmission lines and substations are available to link power, whether future production can be consumed domestically or exported, and the long-term financial liabilities new agreements would impose on the utility.

So far, the NEA has signed PPAs for 404 run-of-the-river projects with a combined capacity of 6,713.44MW, 51 peaking run-of-the-river projects generating 4,186.81MW, one 140MW storage project and 88 solar projects with a combined capacity of 1,055.14MW.

Stakeholders acknowledge that Nepal's electricity system faces a structural imbalance. Hydropower production surges during the monsoon when rivers swell, but generation drops sharply in winter. Because export markets for surplus monsoon electricity remain limited, the NEA says excessive ‘take-or-pay’ commitments could expose it to significant financial risks by requiring payment for electricity regardless of whether it is consumed or sold.

Industry representatives argue that the government must simultaneously improve the country's generation mix and accelerate investment in transmission infrastructure if Nepal is to sustain hydropower growth while protecting both investors and the power utility.

The debate over new PPAs has intensified as electricity generation continues to outpace growth in domestic demand and exports. Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha has repeatedly said that the government will soon decide on reopening PPAs. He also formed a committee to review hydropower licences and PPA policies. Although the committee has submitted its report, the ministry has yet to announce any concrete decisions.

Since April, Shrestha has also directed the Department of Electricity Development to stop issuing new survey licences for hydropower, solar and other power projects pending a policy review. While new applications continue to be accepted, no fresh licences have been issued.

Department records show that applications have been filed for survey licences covering 257 projects with a combined capacity of 12,330.68MW and for generation licences covering another 46 projects with a total capacity of 8,731MW. The department has already issued survey licences for 257 projects with a combined capacity of 12,321MW and generation licences for 360 projects producing 7,336.69MW.

Private developers argue that the current slowdown comes despite Nepal wasting valuable electricity during the monsoon. With around 4,300MW connected to the national grid, they estimate that more than 900MW of power remains unused during peak rainy months because domestic demand and export capacity remain limited.

The NEA, however, avoids describing this electricity as wasted, maintaining that supply and demand must be managed according to system requirements.

Electricity exports have expanded but remain below available capacity. Although Nepal has secured permission to export up to 1,200MW to India and Bangladesh, the NEA says average exports currently stand at about 1,000MW.

Generation capacity continues to grow. During the last fiscal year of 2025-26 alone, 25 hydropower and solar projects with a combined capacity of 560.99MW were connected to the national grid, compared with 434MW added in the fiscal 2024-25. Most of the new generation came from run-of-the-river projects. Although the government had targeted adding 942MW during the year, several projects missed deadlines because of transmission bottlenecks, construction delays and financing constraints.

Among the major additions was the 102MW Middle Bhotekoshi Hydropower Project, promoted by an NEA subsidiary, which began supplying electricity nearly 14 years after construction started. The current fiscal year's budget targets another 1,040MW of additional generation.

Despite rising exports, Nepal still imports electricity during winter because most new projects are run-of-the-river plants that generate far less power during the dry season. Nevertheless, imports have declined significantly.

According to the NEA, Nepal exported electricity worth Rs29.32 billion during the last fiscal year while importing power worth Rs10.22 billion.

Domestic electricity demand is also increasing. Consumption rose by 10.74 percent in the 2024-25 fiscal year, encouraging policymakers to focus on expanding local use alongside exports.

Stakeholders argue that greater domestic consumption would create far higher economic value than exporting electricity itself. "Electricity is a raw material," said Birendra Raj Pandey, president of the Confederation of Nepalese Industries. "If Nepal can consume more electricity at home, we can add value, reduce imports and generate much greater economic benefits."

Pandey said unreliable transmission and distribution infrastructure continues to affect power supply in industrial corridors. "Around 50 to 60 percent of factories still need backup generators," he said. "The government must invest in infrastructure. Instead of exporting energy directly, we should maximise domestic consumption."

Hydropower developers have renewed calls for opening electricity trading to the private sector. Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice-president of the Independent Power Producers' Association Nepal, said developers have already invested heavily in projects that cannot proceed without PPAs.

"The NEA cannot refuse to sign PPAs and at the same time prevent the private sector from trading electricity," he said. "If private companies are allowed to trade power, the burden on the NEA will also ease."

IPPAN estimates that Rs1.243 trillion has already been invested in 7,251MW worth of operational and under-construction hydropower projects, while another Rs66.62 billion has been spent on 576 projects in various phases of survey, design work or licensing with a combined capacity of 27,535MW.

Former IPPAN president Ganesh Karki said policy inconsistency has undermined investor confidence. "Last year's budget stopped PPAs for projects below 10MW. This year's budget reopened them, but implementation has still not begun," he said.

NEA Executive Director Dirghayu Shrestha said the authority's board has formed a committee to examine the reopening of PPAs for projects below 10MW and that future decisions will be based on its recommendations.

Nepal currently imports and exports up to 1,000MW of electricity through the 400kV Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur cross-border transmission line, as well as other 132kV transmission lines. Nepal and India have agreed to increase the import capacity to 1,400MW and the export capacity to 1,650MW through the existing Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur line and the under-construction 400kV Dhalkebar–Sitamarhi transmission line.

Similarly, Nepal and India have agreed that the under-construction Butwal–Gorakhpur cross-border transmission line will initially enable the import of up to 130MW of electricity and the export of up to 200MW.

articles.title: Nepal seeks India’s recognition of NID card as valid travel document
articles.summary:
Nepal’s National Identity (NID) card could soon become another recognised document for travelling to India, with the government seeking New Delhi’s approval to allow its use alongside the citizenship certificate and passport.

The proposal has already been forwarded to the Indian side for consideration, and the Department of Immigration (DoI) is awaiting a formal response, a senior immigration official told the Post.

At present, Nepali citizens travelling to India, particularly by air, must carry either a passport or a citizenship certificate. Likewise, Indian citizens travelling to Nepal are required to present either a passport or an original Indian voter identity card with a photograph, according to the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu.

As the government has made the NID card mandatory for obtaining services at many government offices and in the banking sector, and plans to eventually replace the citizenship certificate with the NID card, the DoI has proposed recognising the NID as a third valid travel document.

“We have already forwarded the proposal to the Indian side through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” said Ram Chandra Tiwari, director general at the DoI.

As soon as an Indian nods, the NID card will work as a third identity card that assists Nepali citizens to India on both land and air routes.

Earlier this week, a team from the Indian Embassy held discussions with Tiwari and other senior DoI officials regarding the proposal. According to another immigration official, the embassy team appeared “positive” about the request and informed Nepali officials that the proposal had already been forwarded to New Delhi for further consideration.

“In the long run, we will have a single identity card replacing the citizenship certificate. It is verified, authentic and technology-friendly,” Tiwari said. “That is why we have requested India to allow the use of the National Identity Card while travelling by both air and land routes.”

A Home Ministry official said that during several bilateral meetings, Nepal and India had also discussed introducing a mechanism to maintain records of cross-border travellers and regulate their movement more systematically.

The NID card contains biometric information, including fingerprints, facial images and iris scans. More than 4.5 million Nepali citizens have already received the card, while around 20 million people have applied for one.

The government has made the NID mandatory for accessing several public services, including passport applications, land registration, opening bank accounts and other government services.

Nepal first launched the National Identity Card programme as a pilot project in Panchthar district and among employees at Singha Durbar in 2009.

“Although all Nepali citizens have not yet received the NID card, it is secure and technology-friendly. Therefore, we have proposed that India allow its use while travelling to and within India,” Tiwari said.

Since citizens of Nepal and India do not require visas to travel between the two countries, both governments currently recognise only a limited number of identity documents issued by their respective authorities. Recognising the NID card would make travel more convenient for Nepali citizens by providing an additional identification option if they do not have a passport or citizenship certificate, Tiwari added.

While the Department of Immigration reports that around 150,000 Nepalis travelled to India last year, there is no official data combining those who crossed the southern border by land and air.

Indian security and foreign policy experts have also raised concerns about strengthening identity checks at border crossings. Writing on X, Professor Brahma Chellaney argues that, given the millions of Nepali citizens living and working in India, fencing or closing the border would be impractical and harmful to bilateral relations.

“The answer is smarter, not tighter, border management: using AI-enabled facial recognition, biometric screening, automated systems and surveillance technology to prevent criminals and terrorists from exploiting the border while keeping it accessible for legitimate travellers.”

Chellaney adds that technology alone is insufficient; effective security requires closer Nepal–India cooperation through joint patrols, intelligence sharing and updated legal mechanisms to facilitate the extradition of fugitives.

articles.title: Provincial alliances crumble as cracks develop in Congress-UML ties
articles.summary:
The Nepali Congress has decided to end its governing alliance with the CPN-UML in all seven provinces. With the party moving to break its partnership with the UML and explore new political alignments, provincial power equations are set for another major change.

The fallout from growing disagreements between the Congress and the UML leaderships at the centre over the future of their provincial alliance became visible on Wednesday.

Shortly after Kamal Bahadur Shah, chief minister of the Congress-led Sudurpaschim Province, dismissed four UML ministers, the UML withdrew its support to his government. In Karnali Province, meanwhile, four Congress ministers submitted their joint resignations to Chief Minister Yamlal Kandel on Wednesday. Congress leaders said ministers serving in UML-led governments in other provinces are also expected to resign by Thursday.

Congress Vice-president Bishwa Prakash Sharma confirmed that the party has decided to walk away from the alliance with the UML. He said the decision followed the UML’s failure to show sincerity over its political approach to the Gen Z protests and the handling of provincial governments.

Under an earlier agreement to rotate leadership in the provinces, Congress had tasked Sharma with negotiating with UML chair KP Sharma Oli. Sharma had been holding both in-person and telephone discussions with Oli.

“When people stay together but no longer feel they truly are, even husbands and wives part ways. Our relationship with the UML had reached a point where it became suffocating, and we felt we had no option but to walk away,” Sharma told Kantipur.

Sharma said Congress would remain in the opposition in the provinces if it failed to reach an understanding with Pushpa Kamal Dahal, coordinator of the Nepali Communist Party (NCP). If an agreement is reached, however, the party would seek to remain in government.

At present, Congress and the UML jointly govern all seven provinces. Congress leads the governments in Madhesh, Bagmati, Sudurpaschim and Gandaki, while the UML heads the governments in Koshi, Lumbini and Karnali.

Amid discussions over a possible new coalition, Congress President Gagan Thapa and NCP coordinator Dahal met on Tuesday. With Congress now set to end its partnership with the UML, Dahal’s NCP has emerged as the decisive force in determining the next round of provincial governments.

During their hour-long meeting, Thapa and Dahal discussed power-sharing arrangements and leadership across all seven provinces. Dahal left for Sri Lanka on Wednesday for a three-day visit after meeting Thapa. Congress leaders said further negotiations on provincial power-sharing will resume only after his return.

NCP leader Narayan Kaji Shrestha said that while discussions had taken place with both Congress and the UML, they had yet to produce any concrete outcome.

“For some time now, both Congress and UML have proposed provincial partnerships. At the time, we were not interested in joining a government merely for power. Now, it seems circumstances may compel us to,” Shrestha said. “So far, we have not decided which party we will align with.”

The attention of both major parties is now centred on NCP coordinator Dahal. As the NCP's support is crucial to forming provincial governments, both Congress and UML have intensified parallel efforts to win over the party. During informal discussions, each side has proposed coalition models based on previous alliances.

Since the 2022 elections, four different coalition arrangements have taken shape: UML-Maoist Centre (now NCP), Congress-Maoist, UML-Maoist, and UML-Congress. Provincial governments have largely mirrored the coalitions formed at the centre.

“The talks have been positive. However, parallel discussions are also taking place between the UML and the NCP on possible left unity and cooperation, so it remains unclear which way Dahal will ultimately lean,” said another Congress office-bearer. “If we fail to reach an understanding with NCP coordinator Dahal, we will sit in the opposition in all provinces.”

Shrestha, however, dismissed suggestions that the NCP was moving towards cooperation or unification with the UML.

“The media has been talking about left unity. In reality, no such discussions or initiatives have taken place,” he said.

As tensions in Sudurpaschim pushed the Congress towards ending its alliance with the UML, Oli also stepped up his engagement with the NCP leadership.

Rajesh Bajracharya, a leader close to UML chief Oli, said the party had concluded that cooperation with the Congress could no longer continue after developments in Sudurpaschim and Karnali.

“I do not have details of what further discussions are taking place on this,” he said.

UML leader Mahesh Bartaula, however, said a section within his party still believes cooperation with the Congress remains necessary given the country’s complex political situation. He argued that collaboration should extend not only to the Congress but also to other parties, including the NCP.

Bartaula said the dispute in Sudurpaschim was triggered primarily by the provincial budget. The UML had demanded changes to the budget tabled by the Congress-led provincial government, arguing that it violated the spirit of the coalition. After the UML decided not to support the budget in the Provincial Assembly, Congress summoned Chief Minister Shah to Kathmandu for consultations.

“We have already called Chief Minister Shah to Kathmandu. You also call your representative and let us discuss a way forward,” another Congress leader recalled telling the UML during recent talks. “But UML chair Oli reportedly responded, ‘Let the Congress defeat the budget in Koshi. I will nominate another UML leader there. Meanwhile, the UML will defeat the budget in Sudurpaschim. Since the chief minister there is close to Sher Bahadur Deuba, you should also propose another name.’ Our leaders considered that approach deeply unpolitical and decided to withdraw from the alliance.”

The Congress had proposed changing leadership in six provinces, excluding Madhesh, in line with an agreement reached on July 1, 2025. The seven-point deal stated: “Provincial governments will be formed in accordance with the spirit of a national consensus government, and development works at the provincial and local levels will be expedited in line with public expectations.”

The agreement implied that changes in the governing arrangement at the centre would be reflected in provincial leadership as well.

Speculation over changes in provincial leadership intensified after the change in Congress leadership. As former president Deuba had appointed close allies as chief ministers, the new leadership under Thapa came under pressure from within the party to replace them.

Following Thapa’s election on March 5, and in line with the understanding between the two parties, preparations began for changes in provincial leadership. Congress Vice-president Sharma spent the past month negotiating with Oli. In earlier rounds of talks, both sides had agreed to go for leadership changes after budget sessions of provincial assemblies.

However, Congress leaders say Oli’s proposal to defeat the budgets in Koshi and Sudurpaschim, coupled with the UML's refusal to hand over the chief minister's post in Koshi, ultimately prompted the party to abruptly end the alliance.

Bartaula maintained that, given the common ground shared by Congress and the UML on key national issues in Parliament, continued cooperation in the provinces would remain beneficial.

“Discussions are ongoing, but nothing has been finalised. We are not in a position where we must distance ourselves from the Congress, and the party is still deliberating the matter,” he said. “The Sudurpaschim incident has certainly widened the rift, but it could have been resolved. We do not believe our relationship with Congress should end over that issue alone.”

The provincial arithmetic

In the 93-member Koshi Provincial Assembly, 47 seats are required to form a government. The Congress holds 29 seats and the NCP 17. Together, they command 46 seats—one short of a majority. With the Janata Samajbadi Party (JSP) holding just one seat, this coalition would have only a slim majority, making the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), with five seats, a potential kingmaker.

The UML currently leads the provincial government. If the NCP sides with the UML, the existing coalition would remain comfortably in power, with the UML’s 40 seats and the NCP’s 17 giving them a combined strength of 57.

In the 110-member Bagmati Provincial Assembly, 56 seats are needed for a majority. A Congress-NCP alliance would comfortably command 65 seats, with Congress holding 37 seats and the NCP 28.

A UML-NCP alliance, however, would fall one seat short of the majority mark, with a combined strength of 55 seats. It would therefore require the support of either the RPP, which has 13 seats, or the Hamro Nepali Party, which has two.

In the 60-member Gandaki Provincial Assembly, 31 seats are needed to form a government. A Congress-NCP coalition would enjoy a comfortable majority with 35 seats, comprising the Congress’s 27 and the NCP’s eight.

A UML-NCP alliance, by contrast, would have only 29 seats—22 from the UML and seven from the NCP—leaving it two short of the majority threshold. In that scenario, the RPP’s two seats would become decisive.

In the 83-member Lumbini Provincial Assembly, 42 seats are required to form a government. The Congress and the NCP together hold 40 seats—27 and 13 respectively—leaving them two seats short of a majority.

To form a government, the alliance would need the support of smaller parties such as the JSP, Janamat Party and Loktantrik Samajbadi Party (LSP), which hold two seats each, or the Janata Samajbadi Party-Nepal, which has one seat.

A UML-NCP alliance, on the other hand, would command exactly 42 seats, giving it the narrowest possible majority.

In the 40-member Karnali Provincial Assembly, 21 seats are needed for a majority. The Congress and the NCP hold 14 seats each, giving them a combined strength of 28, which makes a comfortable majority.

A UML-NCP alliance would also be able to form a government, with the UML’s 10 seats and the NCP’s 14 delivering a total of 24.

In the 53-member Sudurpaschim Provincial Assembly, 27 seats are required to form a government. A Congress-NCP alliance would comfortably secure a majority with 33 seats, comprising the Congress’s 18 and the NCP’s 15.

A UML-NCP coalition, however, would have only 26 seats—one short of the majority mark. It would therefore need the support of the Nagarik Unmukti Party, which holds seven seats.

Madhesh is currently governed by a Congress-led coalition comprising itself, the UML, the NCP and Madhesh-based parties.

In the 107-member Provincial Assembly, 54 seats are required for a majority. The Congress and the NCP together hold only 37 seats, while a UML-NCP alliance would command 38.

Neither combination can form a government on its own, making the support of Madhesh-based parties indispensable. The key players are the JSP-Nepal with 16 seats, the Janamat Party with 13, and the Loktantrik Samajbadi Party with nine.

articles.title: Senior justice Malla assumes acting chief justice role amid ongoing leadership row
articles.summary:
On Thursday, Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma left for India on a four-day official visit following an invitation from his Indian counterpart, Surya Kant. Senior-most Justice Sapna Pradhan Malla saw him off at Tribhuvan International Airport, marking her first public appearance alongside Sharma since his appointment. During his absence, Malla assumed the responsibility of acting chief justice, taking charge of the Supreme Court leadership on Friday.

The warm send-off at the airport sparked speculation within legal circles about a potential reconciliation between the two top justices. Malla’s presence was viewed by some as an attempt to mend working relations and move forward together with Chief Justice Sharma.

Following Sharma’s appointment as chief justice, Malla went on a long leave and remained irregular upon her return, notably missing from the constitutional bench where she previously sat as a regular member.

Malla and Sharma’s strained relationship: From bench orders to airport send-off

Malla, the senior-most justice of the apex court, was in line to become Nepal’s second female chief justice after Sushila Karki. Historically, judicial tradition dictated that the senior-most justice succeeded the retiring chief justice.

The Judicial Council recommended a roster of six names, placing Malla at the top. She anticipated her nomination during the Constitutional Council meeting on May 7.

However, the Constitutional Council, chaired by Prime Minister Balendra Shah, bypassed the top three senior justices—Malla, Kumar Regmi, and Hari Prasad Phuyal—and recommended Sharma, who was fourth in seniority.

Speaker DP Aryal, Law Minister Sobita Gautam, and Deputy Speaker Rubi Kumari Thakur supported the prime minister’s proposal, while opposition party leader Bhishma Raj Angdembe and National Assembly Chairman Narayan Dahal filed written disagreements.

Critics argued this ‘pick-and-choose’ approach broke long-standing judicial conventions and undermined judicial independence. Writ petitions challenging the decision as unlawful faced administrative hurdles at the Supreme Court. The court administration rejected filings by senior advocates Dinesh Tripathi and Prem Raj Silwal, withholding formal refusal orders for days.

The dispute peaked on May 18, a day before Sharma’s parliamentary hearing. Petitioners submitted an application to Malla, who was then serving as acting chief justice, alleging that the administration was deliberately withholding orders to block judicial review. Malla issued a three-page order directing the administration to register the petitions by 1 pm that afternoon and schedule a hearing for the following day. Following her directive, key administrative staff, including the chief registrar and registrar, briefly went untraceable.

On May 19, the Parliamentary Hearing Committee unanimously endorsed Sharma. He took charge as the 33rd Chief Justice of Nepal. Displeased with being bypassed by a junior colleague, Malla took 20 days of approved leave. Justice Kumar Regmi welcomed Sharma to the court instead. Malla returned to her judicial duties on June 8.

During their tenure, actions taken by senior justices to stay certain government decisions fueled rumours of political pressure, including threats of impeachment or demands for resignation. Reports circulated within judicial corridors that the government pressured the three bypassed justices to resign, allegedly with Sharma’s backing. These rumours subsided when no formal motion was tabled. However, statements from three international human rights organisations expressing concern over political interference in the judiciary revived public debate on Friday.

The rift between Sharma and Malla also impacted the Judicial Council, stalling key judicial appointments across the Supreme Court, High Courts, and district courts. Tensions appeared to ease slightly on July 16, when Malla attended a Judicial Council meeting and agreed to the transfer of 50 High Court judges and 157 district court judges.

Has their relationship improved?

Speaking to Kantipur on condition of anonymity, five sitting Supreme Court justices presented differing views on whether relations between the top two apex court justices had truly improved. Some described Malla’s presence at the airport as a mere formal duty rather than a gesture of goodwill.

“The impeachment rumours have not completely vanished,” one sitting justice told Kantipur. “Simply seeing someone off at the airport or signing transfer decisions in the Judicial Council does not mean everything is resolved. We must wait and observe how upcoming judicial appointments, bench assignments, and constitutional bench rosters are managed in the coming days.”

Meanwhile, justices considered to be close to Chief Justice Sharma emphasised the necessity of unity to safeguard the institution.

“Internal division and personal friction among justices only weaken the judiciary,” another justice said. “Past precedents show that judicial instability harms the entire system. Justices must sit together, communicate openly with the chief justice, and work collaboratively under his leadership.”

When contacted for comment regarding the reported reconciliation with Sharma, acting Chief Justice Malla declined to comment. “I have no official statement to make on this matter,” she said.

articles.title: Why strong foreign policy starts at home
articles.summary:
Democratic Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, aka AOC, when asked if she will use her House seat as a platform to run for the United States presidency in 2028, said, in her usual forthright manner, that Republicans assume her ambition is ‘positional’. She implies that the assumption that she wants a platform for herself via a high position is a deeply cynical one. Actually, her ambition is much higher. What she wants is healthcare covered by the State, living wages, workers’ rights, women’s rights—changes that will last forever, not a position that is finite.

Today’s leaders in Nepal should take note. While many of us continue to believe that RSP leaders have good intentions, it is also important to keep in mind that politics is not just about position and the heady power that comes with it. It is about bringing about real change. Recently, another outspoken young woman, Sobita Gautam, the current Law Minister, was interviewed at length, where she also emphasised that politics is not about glamour; it is about putting in real work towards change.

As the RSP’s 100 days are over and we are looking towards the upcoming five years, the commitment to strengthening Nepal’s social and economic landscape is crucial to its global and geo-political situation. Our foreign policy has long been dictated by men who have wielded kompromat and used the excuse of realpolitik to fulfil their own interests. With a brand new set of more principled leaders, one hopes that kind of warped behaviour evolves into a more dignified modus operandi.

Regardless of this clean slate, without a long-term strategy of strengthening Nepal itself, our foreign policy will continue to remain feeble. Although landlocked between two behemoth superpowers, Nepal is no longer quite the squishable yam it used to be. To become an economic bridge or ‘buffer’, however, this country must hone its outward strategy with a common-sense approach of multilateralism, shrewd understanding of psychology underscored by strategic intelligence, leading to a steady action-based, long-lasting approach, executed with integrity. These aspects are essential to any sound foreign policy plan but are not nearly enough. Nepal has to be able to generate products that are worth trading so that we can finally negotiate on our own terms.

The obvious options, such as electricity production and export, are not the no-brainers they appear to be. Corruption, transmission infrastructure, procurement challenges, third-country investors and geopolitics, all play a role. The biggest elephant in the room is climate change. Adverse changes in hydrology have already affected many hydropower projects that have come online, and this trend will only continue without an urgent national and global shift in climate policy with actual provisioning, not just sham diplomacy and COP summits in problematic host countries.

Digital transformation is essential, but a thorough SWOT analysis must be conducted before extending that transformation to include exporting processing power and cloud storage. With data centres guzzling water, even with our monsoon surpluses, an investment like this without adequate research could adversely affect Nepal’s water security.

Which leads, of course, to food security. For a country that has so much agricultural promise, Nepal is now importing more food than it exports, and farmers are constantly at the mercy of fertiliser shortages in an increasingly volatile global supply. With no signs of the climate crisis easing, without serious thought towards solutions for securing our water and food supplies, Nepal, already vulnerable, will become cripplingly so. This unpreparedness will only make us ever more malleable on the global political scene, not to mention leaving us without the option to trade for power. The chance to become an agricultural export powerhouse—although decades behind due to malignant short-sightedness—is still possible with the right kind of strategic planning and infrastructure.

The weak education system contributes greatly to our economic situation. Without an outward-looking education plan that concentrates on producing a workforce with global skills, like proficiency with languages, digital familiarity, practical and out-of-the-box thinking (instead of rote skills that will swiftly be rendered obsolete by AI), Nepal will never be able to compete with a far better-trained global workforce. Our youth will go on spending more than they can afford to study abroad, or jump ship the moment they find any, even menial, opportunities abroad, weakening both our output and our communities.

Nepal needs to fully overhaul its byzantine, STEM-heavy education system to prepare for a future where original, ethical, critical and creatively trained minds will be the essential 21st-century skills. These qualities are also vital in the citizens of any country to create a national ethos that is truly liberal, even as it is civic-minded. This is the kind of training that will produce future entrepreneurs and diplomats who are profoundly engaged with Nepal’s languages, culture, domestic intricacies, strengths and weaknesses, in addition to being able to assess complex situations and sift fake news from facts—all crucial now to function at an international level.

Take Korea’s unparalleled soft power in the form of K-Pop, K-Drama and K-Beauty. These homegrown creative industries, drawing on Korea’s historical cultural strengths, have now provided that country with employment, worldwide recognition and an enormous boost in its balance of trade, all the while shoring up their resilience. Such creative industries require very little aside from ideas and intellectual property development for success. Little is imported; everything can be exported.

Investment in these domestically strong industries created an opportunity for strong export and diplomacy. Everyone knows who they are, thanks to these exports. Korea is now recognised for positive creativity instead of its endemic problems of misogyny and low birth rate. One only has to shudder through Han Kang’s The Vegetarian, the 2007 Nobel Prize-winning, searing meta-fable of domestic abuse and women-hating toxic masculinity, to see that Korean culture is not just fresh-faced glass skin, K-pop demon hunters, and happy romances.

With this new government and sincere leadership from the likes of people like Foreign Minister Sishir Khanal, whose pedigree of civil society activism is hard to match, one hopes for more space for marginalised women in diplomatic positions who will represent those who have been historically sidelined, making them the face of the country. Nepal must look inwards to strengthen its own inclusiveness and society even as it navigates the complexity of its geographical and global position by shoring up its own strengths instead of flexing wildly against forces that cannot be matched without doing our own exercises first.

Foreign policy is not about building one’s own social and political capital for personal ambition. It is not about position or glamour. It is about investing in Nepal’s culture and communities, researching and strategising on how to leverage this country’s human, social, natural, financial and physical capital for the benefit of all its 30 million people to negotiate and compete on par with the world in an increasingly globalised landscape.

articles.title: RSP promised to clean up academia. Why the sudden U-turn?
articles.summary:
The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) promised to depoliticise Nepal’s public institutions, particularly universities, by replacing existing office bearers with appointments based on transparency, merit and integrity. However, recent Vice Chancellor (VC) appointments challenge this commitment. Lower-ranked candidates under the government’s own evaluation framework were chosen over higher-ranked individuals, despite concerns regarding their professional credibility, raising serious questions about whether the selection process was genuinely merit-based. Rather than demonstrating a merit-based process, the outcome raises a broader question: Has the Government of Nepal genuinely reformed the way it selects academic leaders, or has it simply redesigned the appearance of the process?

Initially, the VC selection process seemed like a meaningful departure from the past, utilising strategic plans, interviews, a published scoring framework and online public feedback to project fairness and transparency. Collectively, these measures projected the image of a government committed to procedural fairness and institutional transparency.

Yet the credibility of any selection process depends not on the sophistication of its procedures but on the consistency between those procedures and the outcome. Transparency in a democratic government does not require that the highest-scoring candidate always be selected. It does require that when governments depart from the framework they establish, they clearly explain why. Without that explanation, the public is left unable to understand whether the decision reflected legitimate judgment or political influence.

The process itself also raises questions that deserve careful public consideration. If the published scoring model was not intended to influence the final decision substantially, what purpose did it serve? If the government intended to demonstrate that political considerations would no longer shape university appointments, why have the outcomes renewed debate about political influence rather than academic leadership?

Equally important is the composition of the selection process itself. What qualifications were used in selecting the expert panel? Were these individuals the country’s foremost authorities in higher education governance and university administration, and on what basis were they entrusted with evaluating candidates who, in several cases, possessed decades of senior academic and administrative experience?

Finally, if stakeholder perspectives were considered valuable, why was consultation conducted through an unrestricted online survey rather than directed toward those with a direct institutional stake in the university, its faculty, researchers, students, alumni and administrative staff?

Public engagement is an important component of democratic governance, but participation strengthens institutional legitimacy only when it is meaningful. An unrestricted online survey may create the appearance of participation, but it does little to strengthen confidence in decisions involving specialised leadership.

The disappointment over the university appointments is significant because RSP had promised transparency, systems over personalities, and institutions over patronage. Whether the final appointments are justified or not, the process has raised many questions on whether RSP’s promises are being reflected in institutional practice.

The consequences extend well beyond a single appointment. It is about whether Nepal is building institutions that reward intellectual integrity, administrative competence and public service, or institutions that merely perform those values while operating according to a different set of rules. When governments invite accomplished academics to prepare detailed strategic proposals, participate in extensive interviews and compete under published evaluation criteria, they create a reasonable expectation that merit will play a central role in determining the outcome. If that expectation is later undermined, the damage is institutional rather than personal. Such a facade of transparency erodes public confidence more deeply than the opaque systems it was intended to replace.

This is perhaps the greatest cost of performative transparency. Every time governments ask professionals to devote their expertise to elaborate competitions without demonstrating that the published rules genuinely matter, the result is the gradual erosion of intellectual capital. Talented individuals begin to conclude that intellectual preparation, administrative experience and academic achievement are secondary to politics.

Nepal frequently speaks of reversing brain drain, strengthening higher education and building knowledge-based institutions. Those ambitions cannot be realised without public trust. Talented people do not commit their lives to institutions they believe are indifferent to merit. Nepal cannot simultaneously lament the departure of its brightest minds while creating appointment processes that leave many questioning whether professional excellence is genuinely rewarded. Intellectual integrity is sustained not through speeches about reform, but through institutions that consistently demonstrate, through their decisions, that merit matters.

Perhaps the deepest concern is that this culture extends beyond any one government or political party. It points to institutional structures that repeatedly reward loyalty over competence and discourage those who seek to serve through expertise and public service. It is the same old theatrics and game of power and hunger, just a change in the people. Whether it is the old guard or the new wave, the rot is not in the people at the top, but in the soil of the system itself.

Good people can never do good because the system is designed to suffocate them. Those who participated in good faith invested significant time, effort and preparation, believing that integrity, merit and genuine competition still held value within Nepal’s public institutions. If the outcome was ultimately shaped by considerations that outweighed the published process, then those efforts served little purpose beyond legitimising a decision whose reasoning remains unexplained.

Merit-based selection cannot coexist with opaque decision-making. This erodes hope for citizens who value public service, creating the perception that merit is secondary to political calculations. Ultimately, it discourages the principled, qualified individuals Nepal’s public institutions need to attract.

The single request to public leaders is simply this: Be honest.

Governments come and go. Political parties rise and fall. But institutions endure. Their legitimacy depends not on the promises leaders make, but on whether their actions consistently reflect the principles they proclaim.

If Nepal truly seeks to build world-class universities capable of retaining talented scholars, inspiring future generations and reversing the country’s persistent brain drain, then merit cannot simply be celebrated in speeches. It must be visible in the decisions that matter most. Because when the appearance of transparency becomes more important than transparency itself, it is not only merit that dies in the dark. Public trust dies with it.

articles.title: The hidden economic bill of Nepal’s monsoon disasters
articles.summary:
As Nepal enters another monsoon season, overflowing rivers, landslides and disrupted highways have once again become familiar headlines. Every year, rescue helicopters, collapsed bridges, damaged homes and rising death tolls dominate the news for a few days. But families, farmers, businesses and local governments have to bear the economic burden of the disaster even after floodwaters recede.

To better understand this burden, we analysed major weather-related disasters recorded in the internationally recognised EM-DAT database between 2015 and 2025. Our analysis identified 32 major disasters that resulted in 2,042 deaths, 1,681 injuries and affected more than 5.78 million people. Although deaths and the number of people affected are reported for every disaster, household economic losses often remain unmeasured, leaving disaster management focused largely on recovery, rather than prevention.

Only five of the 32 major weather-related disasters recorded between 2015 and 2025 include any estimate of economic damage, meaning around 84 percent have no reported monetary loss figure. Without reliable loss estimates, it is difficult to demonstrate the true cost of disasters or justify greater investment in prevention. Therefore, improving disaster loss data should be a priority for the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and other relevant agencies to support more informed investment decisions.

Floods accounted for 53 percent of Nepal’s major weather-related disasters between 2015 and 2025 and caused the highest number of disaster-related deaths. Nearly four out of every five major weather disasters (78 percent) occurred during the monsoon season, between June and September. This reflects Nepal’s steep terrain, fragile geology and intense monsoon rainfall. Because preparedness has a narrow window, it must begin well before the monsoon arrives, and not after rivers start overflowing. Flood risk reduction should therefore be a central priority in disaster planning, with greater investment in preparedness, early warning systems and resilient infrastructure to reduce future losses.

Because floods account for most major weather disasters, understanding their economic consequences is especially important. Since these losses are poorly measured, it is worth looking closely at what households actually lose. For many rural families, the economic impact of disasters begins even before homes or infrastructure are damaged. Agriculture remains the primary source of livelihood for more than 60 percent of Nepal’s workforce, so when floods or landslides disrupt farming, households lose both immediate income and future harvests.

According to 2024 wage data from Rastriya Shramik Mahasangh Nepal, female agricultural labourers earn an average of Rs553.9 per day and male labourers Rs626.1 per day, meaning a month without work can result in income losses of approximately Rs16,000 to 19,000 per worker, even before crop losses are considered. Because women already earn less, they are more financially vulnerable to these disruptions, highlighting the need for disaster support measures that reflect such differences rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach.

The September 2024 floods illustrate how quickly disaster losses can accumulate. A preliminary government loss and damage assessment found the floods damaged 65,380 hectares of agricultural land, killed nearly 27,000 livestock, and contributed to an estimated Rs46.68 billion in losses across infrastructure, agriculture and other sectors. This reflects a broader national pattern. Nepal’s average annual disaster loss is estimated at Rs2.78 billion, or about 0.08 percent of GDP, but in extreme years losses can reach 2.08 percent of GDP, around 25 times higher than the annual average. This wide variation suggests that a small number of catastrophic disasters account for a disproportionate share of Nepal’s economic losses.

However, these national figures only tell one part of the story and do not fully capture the losses that individuals bear. After the 2015 earthquake, studies estimated that rebuilding a rural house cost an average of Rs681,000, while the government provided a reconstruction grant of only Rs300,000 for a fully damaged home. Families had to cover the remaining Rs381,000 themselves, often through loans that take years to repay or remittances sent home by relatives working abroad, money that could have otherwise gone toward a child’s education or a family’s savings.

This is not a one-time earthquake problem; similar financing gaps reappear after nearly every major flood or landslide, leaving households to absorb much of the recovery cost each time. This can significantly delay recovery, particularly for low-income families with limited financial resources. Government support should therefore be reviewed regularly to keep pace with the real cost of rebuilding, rather than staying fixed for years at a time, so that the financial burden does not fall so heavily on affected households.

The scale of this burden becomes even clearer at the national level. According to research supported by UNDP Nepal, households across Nepal reported Rs415.44 billion in farm and off-farm economic losses over the past five years, an average of roughly Rs83 billion annually. By comparison, the government spent about Rs50 billion per year on disaster response between 2012 and 2020. The difference highlights how much more households absorb than the state invests in prevention. Greater investment in early warning systems, flood risk management and community preparedness could reduce future losses for both families and the government.

The visible damage caused by disasters is often repaired. Roads are rebuilt, bridges restored and schools reopened, but the less visible losses are far harder to recover from. Families lose income, children miss school and debts grow. The evidence shows that investing before disasters occur is more effective than paying for recovery afterwards. According to the UNDRR, every dollar spent on disaster risk reduction can save four to seven dollars in future response and recovery costs. With Nepali households already losing around Rs83 billion to disasters each year, risk reduction should be placed at the centre of disaster management alongside emergency response. Weather disasters are bound to happen. Their financial burden is not.

articles.title: Should Nepal restrict minors’ access to social media?
articles.summary:
Governments across the globe have started to move away from soft guidelines towards hard legal bans on social media access for minors. This global policy shift is driven by mounting evidence of social media-driven mental health crises, addictive platform designs, and rising cybercrime. Australia recently enacted a nationwide ban for those under 16. In Southeast Asia, Indonesia and Malaysia have introduced regulations to block under-16s from social media platforms. From January 2027, France will implement a law banning children under 15 from social media. Under these new rules, every user in France will eventually need to verify their age to access platforms. The United Kingdom and the European Union are currently drafting and deliberating on legislation to protect children in the digital space.

The arguments for such strict regulations are primarily grounded in public health concerns. Social media platforms are designed to be addictive, using features like infinite scrolling and autoplaying feeds to maximise user engagement. Research shows that adolescent brains, still developing impulse control, often cannot self-regulate against these triggers. Excessive screen time is directly linked to rising rates of depression, anxiety and body image issues among teenagers. Beyond mental health, unrestricted access exposes minors to predators, grooming and extortion. Furthermore, late-night notifications and compulsive scrolling disrupt sleep patterns essential for physical development in minors.

Critics of these bans raise several concerns, often secondary to the safety of the minors. Some argue that blanket bans violate the rights of children to information and participation in public life. They claim that youth might lose vital online support networks if they are unable to access social media platforms. Enforcement also carries risks, as mandatory age verification might require users to share sensitive personal information through biometrics and government IDs, creating privacy vulnerabilities. Additionally, tech-savvy teenagers may use VPNs to bypass restrictions, potentially pushing them into even less-regulated and more dangerous online spaces.

In South Asia, the legal landscape is already shifting to meet these threats. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which classifies anyone under 18 as a child, requires verifiable parental consent and bans platforms from tracking or profiling minors. Pakistan and Bangladesh are also engaged in active policy debates regarding nationwide bans for those under 16. Meanwhile, Nepal remains behind the curve and currently has no statutory minimum age for social media access. The current legal framework focuses on content moderation rather than restricting access.

Nepal cannot afford to lag behind any longer. While other nations build digital shields, Nepal’s youth remain exposed. Meanwhile, cybercrime against minors in the country has quadrupled in just three years. The rise of generative AI has worsened the situation, with deepfakes becoming common tools for peer harassment. The human cost in Nepal is already significant. One in three Nepali children has expressed a willingness to meet online ‘friends’ in person. Of those who do, nearly 28 percent encounter abusive behaviour. Nearly 40 percent of girls have received unsolicited explicit messages or images online. Mental health is suffering, with over 34 percent of teenagers spending up to six hours a day on social media. This leads to anxiety and academic decline.

Nepal must start an active and urgent discourse on social media regulation for minors. The country’s youth are navigating a digital minefield without adequate protection or literacy. The rise in online-to-offline predatory behaviour and AI-driven manipulation demands a stronger response than mere content moderation. Policymakers need to examine the models used across the world and draft one suitable for Nepal. Waiting for the problem to solve itself is not an option when the well-being of an entire generation is at stake. It is time for Nepal to build a legal framework that ensures child safety on social media platforms.

articles.title: EXHIBIT REVIEW: On recollections of homeland
articles.summary:
Standing before the large-scale artworks of Sanod Maharjan brings a peculiar, almost incomprehensible emotion that, with all its abstraction and sublimity, surprises the artist himself.

“In multiple instances, I have found new meanings in my art,” says Maharjan. “Be it while revisiting them long after I pass a particular momentary conscience, or through conversations with people explaining their perspectives.”

Fragments of yellow, green, purple, red, and black are enveloped in different forms of life in ‘Ek Hul Batas’, avoiding anything larger than itself. With that, the exhibit’s poignancy takes different shapes with each passing viewer.

Perhaps it is this artistic freedom that Maharjan gives both to his audience and to himself that makes his artworks particularly provocative with every viewing. They are placed between intention and spontaneity. Every stroke reflects the artist’s impulse, yet strangely enough, it suggests a conscious choice.

While observing ‘Ek Hul Batas VI', a 121*200 cm artwork featuring layers of oil pastel colours; bright and dimmed and strokes; horizontal, vertical, thick, thin, continuous and fragmented, we gather a point of view from the midst of a forest, witnessing the leaves drift with the wind.

When asked why he used a particular colour, length, breadth and height for a stroke, Maharjan avoids concrete answers as he avoids forms in his abstraction. “This was a calling, a give-and-take relationship, and I allowed myself to wonder and play,” he says.

With his abstractions, a message emerges. To be creative is to avoid being careful.

“Particularly in this one, initially I tried giving it a form and composition – an irresistible urge for an art student. And that is where I lost its meaning,” he says.

The recurring motifs of rivers, wind, land, forest, and leaves imply a lingering presence of Maharjan’s birthplace, Tistung. “I paint as a way of listening to my homeland,” he says. “I left Tistung when I was two, and all I have are the memories, which I try to present in my art.”

“‘Ek Hul Batas’ is about the stories, places and people I wish to remember,” he adds.

And every articulation of his reminisce depicts the tangibility of wind [batas], which becomes the most memorable motif of this exhibit. In this play of memories and colours, Maharjan traces the presence and absence of his grandmother. “It feels as though my grandmother is sending me a message through these winds,” he says.

In different canvases, the colours hold similar meanings. Emotions that yellow carries in ‘Ek Hul Batas VI’ persist in his other artworks. What changes is the reason to create.

Standing in front of ‘Ek Hul Batas IV’, a 152*304 cm artwork, which depicts a rather tumultuous state with more muddled and navy strokes than any other, I ask, “Working on this large paper, do you feel a sense of transformation from beginning to end?”

To which he says, “A lot.”

“Along the way, I find myself,” he adds.

In ‘Ma Chu La I’, the ends of paper meet, making it a trunk–like structure of a tree standing on the bundled-up dried leaves in one corner of the gallery. We find the strokes again – yellow, blue, pink, purple. While they come all at once on the paper, none overwhelms the other, as though, even in chaos, thoughts arrive in harmony.

“A human being does not exist in isolation, and neither does a tree,” Maharjan shares. “Placing one here ultimately amounts to the presence of the entire forest.”

The dried leaves also suggest an environmental consciousness. While he gently walks on them, following the crisp sound of nature, he says, almost like an ode, “People, especially grandmothers, had preserved the environment in the past.”

On the other side of the gallery, Maharjan’s 33 artworks, painted since 2017, lie not so detached from his latter creations. Multiple brown-tinted papers are also pasted on the walls, with his letters to the personified places and flowers, particularly rhododendron, as metaphors for humans.

‘Soliset’ [oil on wood panel] gives a sublime introspection of the moment. The point of view emerges from the middle of a river, and the paint depicts what the eyes saw – rocks, leaves, trees, water. The river converges toward the middle of the panel, and on it are the reflections of the trees with rocks underneath its ripples. “I was partially submerged in the river while painting this,” Maharjan says.

While bringing the live art of nature to the wooden canvas, painting also helps him imagine a world beyond what is prescribed. In ‘Ma yaa chu’, with a notable demonstration of light and shadow onto the hills of Tistung, Maharjan imagines a colourful and subtle end of a rainbow towards its right edge.

“A rainbow is something I had never witnessed there,” he recalls. “Therefore, I pictured one and painted it.”

Back to his abstraction, we detect a rather unique piece, mostly because of its title ‘Ouiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii’ and equally because of its form.

A half-horizontal curve of a hill overlapping a second one with a diagonal division depicts an asymmetrical dynamic contrast between light and dark fields. A bright, radiant light source of the setting sun lies near the top-centre notch, drawing the eye immediately upward before tracing through the magenta, blues, deep purples and violet tones of the hills. “It's the red glow of the setting sun,” says Maharjan. “Right after finishing the painting, I had the urge to shout Ouiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii.”

With him shunning a distinctive form in most of his abstract paintings, this one stands out as he simply accepts the presence of the two hills with a remarkable light composition. This change feels as though he encountered something that he had chased for a long time. Perhaps it was his peace, a solicitude within the chaos of his abstraction.

Maharjan persistently carries the nature within him, letting it gently embrace his canvases, his memories, wonder, imagination, creativity, and also his profession.

“I am a full-time farmer and a part-time artist,” he says.

Ek Hul Batas

articles.title: Aesthetic Dance Studio Presents ‘Suresh Mishra Memorial Award’
articles.summary:
Aesthetic Dance Studio has announced the second edition of the Suresh Mishra Memorial Award, an annual initiative established in memory of the late dance educator Suresh Mishra. The event will be held on 29th July at the EK Theatre.

Organised annually on the occasion of Guru Purnima (Teacher's Day), the award recognises individuals who have made meaningful contributions to the field of dance. It honours artists, teachers, choreographers, and other members of the dance community whose commitment and vision continue to strengthen the art form in Nepal.

"Our director, Namrata KC, was one of Suresh Mishra Sir's students and shared a deep bond with him. That connection inspired us to establish this award in his memory," said Akrist Khadka of Aesthetic Dance Studio. "From the very beginning, we decided this would never be a one-time initiative. We committed ourselves to organising it every year so that his legacy continues to inspire the dance community."

Following its inaugural edition last year, the ceremony returns with the theme 'The Legacy That Dances On', celebrating Mishra's lasting influence while encouraging the next generation of dance practitioners. According to the organisers, the initiative seeks to preserve his legacy by recognising those working to develop and advance Nepal's dance sector.

This year's programme will also feature performances by dancers and artists from various dance studios, bringing together members of the dance community to celebrate creativity, collaboration, and artistic expression.

articles.title: BOOK REVIEW: Nothing is quite what it seems in ‘Paridhi’
articles.summary:
If I had to sum up Uma Subedi’s new novel ‘Paridhi’ in one word, I think the word would be ‘trippy’. The novel has many all too realistic aspects, and yet, almost throughout the whole story, the reader is left wondering about what exactly is going on.

The story centres around ‘Arya’, who is herself a writer, a playwright to be exact. She has, however, grown tired of playwriting. Not playwriting exactly, but everything surrounding it – the casting, the direction, and the stage setting – has tired Arya. 'Paridhi', she says to her closest friend, Sambhavi, will be her last.

From the get-go, the novel establishes a sort of non-realism. In the very opening scene of the first half of the book, titled ‘Arya’, readers learn that Arya likes to watch the sun come up every morning. As she does, a voice tells her that it is time for her to 'realise her life’ and that just like how the sun comes up every morning, ‘life is not always dark. If one patiently waits, light comes back again.’

The reader is left to think about how best to understand this voice, but the story moves quickly and gives much more to be thought about.

In the very next scene, Arya is on her scooter trying to get somewhere important (we will return to where) as soon as she can, all the while being followed by a car. 'Followed' is not exactly correct; it would imply the car was behind her, but the car is, in fact, right next to her, intruding into the other lane and keeping pace with her scooter. If she slows down, so does the car, and if she speeds up, the car does too. And in the car are three people, all masked; the masks portraying some nature of sad and distressed faces.

Soon after, the car then crashes, in a bizarre way at that. Instead of the injured or perhaps even dead passengers bleeding dark red blood, they bleed the seven colours of the rainbow – at least as Arya sees it, and that is an important theme in the book: the theme of perception.

It is hard for readers to say what really has transpired in the real world, the world of the five senses, and what has simply occurred in someone’s head. Readers learn that Arya was orphaned at a young age, and yet she narrates some memories of her parents, memories that end in them apparently disappearing into thin air or being accused by bystanders of being ghosts, images of dead people.

Subedi’s writing creates a sense of thrill, of almost impending disaster, and the readers are promised this possible disaster from the start. The novel is set on ‘Bhadra 19’, somewhere in early September. The day is important because it is the day that Arya’s friend ‘Asmita’, after whom the second half of the novel is titled, is set to commit suicide. Asmita’s house is where Arya is rushing to get to in the early morning of Bhadra 19 when the crash occurs.

Despite its deeply philosophical themes of consciousness and perception, Subedi’s writing is plain and easy to follow, even for an out-of-habit reader of Nepali like myself. Also noteworthy is Subedi’s decision to use various loanwords throughout her writing.

For example, in the scene with the car crash, Arya is said to ‘notice’ the masked passengers in the car next to her, which itself is said to be driving in the other ‘lane’. The language is quite contemporary. This type of language adds a sense of realism to an otherwise fantastic story. The characters use social media and mobile apps, and they meet up at cafes to catch up. Again, quite contemporary.

And yet, it is difficult to visualise the story as occurring in the same world as the one readers occupy. The colours feel a little grey, the words feel dreamy, and the story hazy. That is the beauty of Subedi’s writing. The readers are seamlessly transported into the mind of the character, who seems to live in their own words.

Arya is shadow writing Asmita’s autobiography. Sudebi first says she is 'ghostwriting' the autobiography; she then translates it to ‘pret-writing’ in the next sentence. A pret is a type of ghost in Nepali folklore. The decision to describe Arya as Ashmita’s pret-writer feels intentional on the writer’s part – foreshadowing of sorts.

The last part of the book, three short chapters, is titled 'Shadow Realm'. At the end of the dreamlike story, Subedi begins to tie her knots together. In the shadow realm chapter, Arya begins to find answers for many questions and occurrences. At the end, readers learn from the horse’s mouth itself (the wonderful author Uma Subedi) what they would have definitely come to suspect in reading: that something is definitely off with Arya.

Author: Uma Subedi

Publisher: Sangri-La Books

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.
